name: deficiency of il1 receptor antagonist
aliases: deficiency of the interleukin-1 receptor antagonist

clinicalPearls: Autosomal recessive disorder caused by loss-of-function IL1RN variants that abolish functional interleukin-1 receptor antagonist, leaving interleukin-1 alpha and interleukin-1 beta signalling unopposed.
Presents in the neonatal period with a triad of pustular skin disease, sterile multifocal osteomyelitis and periostitis, and marked systemic inflammation.
Skin involvement ranges from scattered pustules to generalised pustulosis with an ichthyosiform appearance, and nail changes such as pustular onychomadesis are characteristic.
Bone disease produces painful swelling with radiographic multifocal osteolytic lesions, periosteal new bone, widening of the anterior rib ends and balloon-like expansion of ribs and clavicles.
Fever is often absent or only low grade despite a striking acute-phase response, which can be a diagnostic clue distinguishing it from infection and from many other autoinflammatory syndromes.
Recombinant interleukin-1 receptor antagonist replacement is dramatically effective and life-saving, essentially replacing the missing protein.
Agents that block only interleukin-1 beta give a less complete response because interleukin-1 alpha signalling also contributes to disease.
Founder loss-of-function variants have been described in several geographically distinct populations, aiding targeted genetic testing.
reference.pathophysiology: The interleukin-1 receptor antagonist is a naturally occurring inhibitor that competes with interleukin-1 alpha and interleukin-1 beta for binding to the type 1 interleukin-1 receptor without triggering signalling. Loss-of-function IL1RN variants remove this brake, so even physiological amounts of interleukin-1 drive unopposed and amplified receptor signalling. The result is intense innate immune activation with neutrophil recruitment to skin and bone, producing sterile pustulosis, multifocal osteomyelitis and periostitis, and a vigorous systemic acute-phase response. Because both interleukin-1 alpha and interleukin-1 beta act on the receptor, complete control requires blockade at the receptor level rather than neutralisation of a single ligand.
additionalDifferentials: Deficiency of the interleukin-36 receptor antagonist (DITRA) with generalised pustular psoriasis
Chronic recurrent multifocal osteomyelitis and chronic non-bacterial osteomyelitis
additionalInvestigations: IL1RN gene sequencing for biallelic loss-of-function variants, including targeted testing for known founder alleles
Skeletal survey for multifocal osteolytic lesions, periostitis and rib-end widening
Skin biopsy demonstrating intraepidermal and subcorneal neutrophilic pustules
Bone biopsy and cultures to confirm sterility and exclude infective osteomyelitis
Acute-phase reactants and full blood count showing a neutrophilic leucocytosis
Blood and tissue cultures to exclude infection before and during immunomodulatory therapy
redFlags: Respiratory distress from thoracic involvement or interstitial lung disease in a neonate
Widespread pustulosis with systemic inflammation mimicking overwhelming sepsis
Multifocal bone lesions in an infant that are repeatedly culture negative
Clinical deterioration or incomplete response when only interleukin-1 beta is blocked
reference.prognosis: Untreated disease carries a high risk of severe morbidity and death from uncontrolled systemic inflammation and its complications. Prompt recombinant interleukin-1 receptor antagonist replacement usually induces rapid and sustained remission with a good long-term outlook.
pitfalls: Mistaking sterile multifocal osteomyelitis for bacterial infection and pursuing prolonged antibiotics
Being reassured by the frequent absence of high fever and underestimating the severity of inflammation
Expecting a full response from interleukin-1 beta-selective blockade rather than receptor-level antagonism
Confusing the phenotype with the clinically overlapping deficiency of the interleukin-36 receptor antagonist
references: Textbook of Pediatric Rheumatology, Cassidy (current edition)
management: Definitive replacement with recombinant interleukin-1 receptor antagonist (anakinra) to block both interleukin-1 alpha and beta signalling at the receptor, restoring the missing inhibitor and inducing rapid, life-saving remission

Consider longer-acting interleukin-1 blockade (canakinumab or rilonacept) where adherence or sustained control is problematic, recognising receptor-level blockade gives the most complete disease control
Supportive care with skin and wound care for pustulosis, analgesia for bone pain, and nutritional support during the systemic inflammatory illness
Serial monitoring of acute-phase reactants and skeletal imaging to titrate therapy and track osteomyelitis, periostitis and bone remodelling
Exclude and treat intercurrent infection before and during immunomodulation, taking blood and tissue cultures, since sepsis can mimic or complicate a flare
Coordinate care across paediatric rheumatology, dermatology, orthopaedics and neonatology
Genetic counselling with IL1RN sequencing and screening of at-risk relatives given autosomal recessive inheritance
